recent_posts.title: From Undefined to Defined: Using std::launder in C++
recent_posts.summary: A deep dive into C++17's std::launder, explaining when and why it's needed to avoid undefined behavior when using placement new. Covers scenarios where the compiler's optimizer can make incorrect assumptions about pointer contents — particularly with const members or type-erased buffers — and shows how std::launder acts as an optimization fence. Also contrasts std::launder with reinterpret_cast, std::bit_cast, and std::start_lifetime_as in a summary table.

recent_posts.title: What reinterpret_cast doesn't do
recent_posts.summary: A deep dive into a common C++ misconception: that reinterpret_cast converts an object from one type to another. In reality, reinterpret_cast only converts the pointer type — it does not create a new object or start its lifetime. Accessing the resulting pointer as the new type is undefined behavior. The post contrasts this with std::start_lifetime_as (C++23), which properly starts the lifetime of a new object in a given memory region without invoking constructors or destructors, making it the correct tool for type punning. A summary table compares reinterpret_cast, std::bit_cast, and std::start_lifetime_as and their appropriate use cases.

recent_posts.title: Why calling virtual member functions in a C++ constructor is unsafe
recent_posts.summary: A C++ Insights episode explaining why calling virtual member functions from a constructor is dangerous. Through examples, it demonstrates the pitfalls of this pattern, which stems from how C++ constructs objects and resolves virtual dispatch during construction.

recent_posts.title: Best performance of a C++ singleton
recent_posts.summary: A deep dive into C++ singleton performance, comparing block-local static variables versus static data members, and user-declared versus user-defined constructors. When a user-defined constructor is required, the block-local static approach forces the compiler to insert guard variables and locking calls (__cxa_guard_acquire/__cxa_guard_release), adding overhead. Using a private static data member avoids these locks entirely. If the default constructor can be defaulted, both approaches produce equivalent assembly. The recommendation: use static data members when a custom constructor is needed, and block-local statics otherwise.

recent_posts.title: Resetting singleton objects using private defaulted move operations in C++
recent_posts.summary: A C++ technique for resetting singleton objects to their default state by using private defaulted copy/move operations. The pattern creates a new object and moves it into the current instance, ensuring the object returns to a default-constructed state without manually duplicating destructor logic. This approach keeps destructors unchanged while guaranteeing consistent reset behavior, though the author now recommends using public deleted operations as the default choice.

top_posts.title: Write modern code with features of C++17 and C++20
top_posts.summary: Transitioning from older C++ standards to C++17 and C++20 can be challenging due to the plethora of new features and syntax changes. This includes structured bindings in C++17 for more intuitive variable declaration, concepts, and ranges in C++20 for better data manipulation. The post highlights the importance of effectively applying these new features and keeping skills up-to-date. A new course, 'Programming C++17 to C++20', is introduced to help developers understand and utilize these modern language features with practical examples and exercises.

top_posts.title: Why is C++23 called 23?
top_posts.summary: C++23, despite being published in 2024, is named based on the planned completion year, following a release train model where new standards are introduced every three years. WG21 completes the standardization, then passes it to ISO for publication. Vendors often implement features from drafts using temporary naming schemes before adopting the official standard names.

top_posts.title: How to use a constexpr std::string
top_posts.summary: C++20 introduced constexpr std::vector and std::string in the Standard Template Library (STL). While creating a string at compile-time and transferring it to runtime is not supported, there are still useful applications. One such use case is creating constexpr functions for compile-time operations, like a decoder for SMS payloads. Despite the limitations, constexpr std::string can be beneficial for certain applications, including compile-time testing with static_assert.

top_posts.title: Forward declaring a type in C++: The good, and the bad
top_posts.summary: Forward declaring types in C++ (incomplete types) can significantly reduce compile times by avoiding header includes, but comes with serious pitfalls. Using delete on an incomplete type causes undefined behavior because the compiler assumes a trivial destructor when it doesn't know the full type definition. The article demonstrates this with a practical example where a destructor never gets called, and provides solutions like using static_assert with sizeof or relying on STL utilities that require complete types. C++26 addresses this UB through P3144R0.

top_posts.title: C++ for embedded systems: constexpr and consteval
top_posts.summary: Learn how modern C++ features like constexpr and consteval can enhance the code quality for embedded systems. The post explores parsing MAC addresses, using std::array for memory safety, std::expected for error handling, and the implementation of user-defined literals for compile-time evaluations.
